newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU expects new rescue plan for C. Lyonnais.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU expects new rescue plan for C. Lyonnais.

text.p: Wary of seeing France's embattled Credit Lyonnais getting any more subsidies, the European Commission said on Tuesday it would react quickly to an expected new French fresh request to rescue the bank.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert was to hold a news conference on the issue on Wednesday at 1015 GMT in expectation that new "information" on a proposed bailout was to be provided by Paris later on Tuesday.

A Commission official said the Commission had not yet received any oral or written plan to soften the terms of a restructuring programme agreed for the state-controlled bank in July 1995. But it is was expected.
There has been mounting speculation that Credit Lyonnais, once the world's largest bank outside Japan, will need a third salvage plan to avoid an humiliating plunge back into the red.

The bank was bailed out by the French state in 1992. In 1995, the Commission agreed to a multiannual plan involving maximum subsidies of 45 billion francs ($8.78 billion) on the condition that it shared part of the restructuring costs, sold 35 percent of its foreign assets was privatised.
It particularly insisted that the bank make a below-market rate loan to finance the state-backed vehicle CDR that took over 130 billion francs of its ailing assets.
Any change to the 1995 plan must get the EU's green light.
Commission sources said there was outrage at reports of yet another rescue plan for the bank and pledged that it could only be approved under very tough conditions.
This could involve the selling of more assets than initially agreed in 1995, an official said, referring in particular to the bank's profitable German subsidiary Bank Fuer Gemeinwirtschaft (BFG).
"This is truly scandalous and should only be allowed if Credit Lyonnais agrees to sell its German unit," the official said.

The bank is expected to announce half-year losses on Thursday unless it secures changes to last year's plan that would cancel retroactively to last January charges incurred in financing the loan to CDR, a Paris source close to the talks said on Monday.
The bank accumulated losses of 21 billion French francs between 1992 and 1994. It eked out a 13 million franc profit in 1995 thanks to the two consecutive rescue plans.
Under the 1995 plan, the Credit Lyonnais must sell at least 35 percent of its foreign assets, including a substantial part of its European banking network, by the end of 1998.

Only last week, the Commission sharply questioned France on compliance with the terms of the plan, saying it had evidence that the bank had bought back cheaply a banking unit Societe de Banque Occidentale, after it benefited from a cash injection by CDR.
